detail: Between 5% and 10% below the high counts as a pullback, and the S&P 500 closed at 7,340.53 on Tuesday, about 6.1% below its record close of 7,818.93 on 6 October. It has now fallen four days running to its lowest close since late July; dips of this size happen in most years.
source: CNBC and Motley Fool closing figures, 17 Nov; record close from Anadolu and EdgeX, 6 Oct

detail: Breadth was narrow on Tuesday: at midday CNBC counted 679 Nasdaq shares at new 52-week lows against 38 at new highs, with fallers outnumbering risers by about 2.7 to 1. When most shares fall together, the selling is wide rather than limited to a few big names.

Above 4.5% counts as high, and the US 10-year yield dipped to about 5.10% on Tuesday from 5.12% as nervous investors bought safe government bonds. Safe bonds paying over 5% set a high bar for shares to beat.
source: CNBC and The Closing Print closing figures, 17 Nov

detail: Markets expect rates to go up: futures now price a quarter-point Fed rise on 9 December as certain, and traders see about a 90% chance of a Bank of England rise on 17 December. Higher rates make borrowing dearer and tend to weigh on share prices, especially fast-growing companies.
source: Fed funds futures via Barchart, 17 Nov; LSEG data via Reuters, 17 Nov

detail: Above $90 a barrel counts as expensive, and Brent crude settled 0.8% higher at $93.14 on Tuesday as attacks on ships near the Strait of Hormuz continued. Dear oil keeps pressure on inflation, which is one reason central banks are raising rates.
source: ICE settlement via DTN and Xinhua, 17 Nov
